evidence: practice-only: fixing and building sentences; it changes no capability estimate

topics.name: Pronoun forms: I and me, myself

items.sentence: My brother plays football.
items.rule: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

items.sentence: We live in India.
items.rule: Names of places start with a capital letter.

items.sentence: I saw [a] elephant at the zoo.
items.rule: Use "an" before a vowel sound: an elephant.

items.sentence: She has [an] red umbrella.
items.rule: Use "a" before a consonant sound: a red umbrella.

items.sentence: He ate [a] apple after lunch.
items.rule: Use "an" before a vowel sound: an apple.

items.sentence: There are three [box] on the table.
items.rule: Words ending in x take -es: boxes.

items.sentence: The two [baby] are sleeping.
items.rule: Change y to ies: baby, babies.

items.sentence: I brushed my [tooths] this morning.
items.rule: Tooth is irregular: one tooth, two teeth.

items.sentence: The dogs [is] barking loudly.
items.rule: A plural subject takes "are": the dogs are.

items.sentence: My sister [like] mangoes.
items.rule: With he, she or one person, add -s: she likes.

items.sentence: We [was] late for school.
items.rule: "We" takes "were".

items.sentence: Ravi is my friend. [She] is ten years old.
items.rule: Ravi is a boy, so the pronoun is "he".

items.sentence: The girls lost [her] ball.
items.rule: "The girls" is plural, so use "their".

items.sentence: Give the book to [I].
items.rule: After "to", use "me".

items.sentence: Yesterday we [play] cricket.
items.rule: "Yesterday" needs the past: played.

items.sentence: She [goed] to the market.
items.rule: Go is irregular: go, went.

items.sentence: I [eated] two idlis.
items.rule: Eat is irregular: eat, ate.

items.sentence: The books are [in] the table.
items.rule: Things rest on a table.

items.sentence: We go to school [in] Monday.
items.rule: Use "on" with days: on Monday.

items.sentence: He was born [on] March.
items.rule: Use "in" with months: in March.

items.sentence: I like tea and coffee.
items.rule: "And" joins two things.

items.sentence: He ran fast but missed the bus.
items.rule: "But" joins two ideas that do not match.

items.sentence: Where do you live?
items.rule: A question starts with a question word and ends with a question mark.

items.sentence: Can you swim?
items.rule: In a question the helping verb comes first.

items.sentence: She sings [beautiful].
items.rule: An adverb of manner tells how: beautifully.

items.sentence: He ran [quick] to the gate.
items.rule: An adverb of manner often ends in -ly: quickly.

items.sentence: We often play chess in the evening.
items.rule: An adverb of frequency such as "often" goes before the main verb.

items.sentence: The children are playing outside.
items.rule: An adverb of place tells where: outside.

items.sentence: He drives very [careful] in the rain.
items.rule: "Very" can strengthen an adverb: very carefully.

items.sentence: We stayed inside because it was raining.
items.rule: "Because" gives the reason.

items.sentence: Although he was tired, he finished his homework.
items.rule: "Although" joins two ideas that seem to pull apart.

items.sentence: I was hungry, [but] I ate a sandwich.
items.rule: "So" shows the result.

items.sentence: Take an umbrella [so] it may rain.
items.rule: "Because" gives the reason.

items.sentence: The train arrives [on] six o'clock.
items.rule: Use "at" with clock times.

items.sentence: She is good [in] drawing.
items.rule: We say "good at".

items.sentence: He divided the sweets [between] the five children.
items.rule: Use "among" for more than two; "between" for two.

items.sentence: We walked [between] the forest for an hour.
items.rule: "Through" means from one side of something to the other.

items.sentence: Hurray! We have won the match.
items.rule: An interjection shows sudden feeling and takes an exclamation mark.

items.sentence: Oh no! I forgot my lunch box.
items.rule: An interjection shows sudden feeling: here, dismay.

items.sentence: Wow! What a beautiful rainbow!
items.rule: "Wow" shows wonder.

items.sentence: Alas! The old tree has fallen.
items.rule: "Alas" shows sorrow.

items.sentence: Please look [on] this word in the dictionary.
items.rule: "Look up" means to find information.

items.sentence: Please turn [of] the lights when you leave.
items.rule: "Turn off" means to stop a light or machine.

items.sentence: We must not give [in] hope.
items.rule: "Give up" means to stop trying or let go.

items.sentence: She takes [up] her mother: they have the same smile.
items.rule: "Take after" means to be like an older family member.

items.sentence: The police will look [up] the matter.
items.rule: "Look into" means to examine.

items.sentence: A stitch in time saves nine.
items.rule: It means: fix a small problem now, before it grows.

items.sentence: Actions speak louder than words.
items.rule: It means: what you do matters more than what you say.

items.sentence: Honesty is the best policy.
items.rule: It means: it is always better to tell the truth.

items.sentence: Do not count your chickens before they hatch.
items.rule: It means: do not depend on something before it happens.

items.sentence: The [boys] room is upstairs; three boys share it.
items.rule: For a plural ending in s, the apostrophe comes after the s: boys'.

items.sentence: The [childrens] park is closed.
items.rule: "Children" is plural without s, so add 's.

items.sentence: This pencil is [my].
items.rule: When no noun follows, use "mine".

items.sentence: That house is [their].
items.rule: When no noun follows, use "theirs".

items.sentence: The dog wagged [it's] tail.
items.rule: "Its" shows belonging; "it's" means "it is".

items.sentence: Ravi is [tall] than his brother.
items.rule: To compare two, add -er: taller than.

items.sentence: This is the [better] book in the library.
items.rule: To compare more than two, use the superlative: best.

items.sentence: She runs [fast] than her sister.
items.rule: To compare two actions, add -er: faster than.

items.sentence: This puzzle is [difficulter] than the last one.
items.rule: Long adjectives take "more": more difficult.

items.sentence: Of all the singers, Meena sang the [more] sweetly.
items.rule: Of more than two, use "most".

items.sentence: I [cant] find my shoes.
items.rule: The apostrophe stands for the missing letters: can't.

items.sentence: She [does'nt] like bitter gourd.
items.rule: The apostrophe replaces the o of "not": doesn't.

items.sentence: [Its] raining, so take an umbrella.
items.rule: "It's" means "it is".

items.sentence: They [wont] come to the party.
items.rule: "Will not" becomes "won't".

items.sentence: She [breaked] the glass yesterday.
items.rule: Break is irregular: break, broke, broken.

items.sentence: He has [ate] all the sweets.
items.rule: After has or have, use the third form: eaten.

items.sentence: We [buyed] vegetables from the market.
items.rule: Buy is irregular: buy, bought.

items.sentence: The bell has already [rang].
items.rule: Ring, rang, rung: after "has" use rung.

items.sentence: I have never [saw] snow.
items.rule: See, saw, seen: after "have" use seen.

items.sentence: Look! The baby is [sleep].
items.rule: The continuous tense is "is" with verb-ing.

items.sentence: They were [swim] when it started to rain.
items.rule: The past continuous is "were" with verb-ing.

items.sentence: She was writing a letter when the phone rang.
items.rule: The past continuous shows an action going on when another happened.

items.sentence: I am [writeing] a story.
items.rule: Drop the e before -ing: writing.

items.sentence: Each of the boys [have] a bat.
items.rule: "Each" is singular: each has.

items.sentence: The news [are] good today.
items.rule: "News" is singular.

items.sentence: My friends and I [am] going to the fair.
items.rule: People joined by "and" take "are".

items.sentence: Neither of the answers [are] correct.
items.rule: "Neither" is singular.

items.sentence: One of my shoes [are] missing.
items.rule: The subject is "one", so the verb is singular.

items.sentence: "Where are you going?" asked Ravi.
items.rule: Spoken words go inside quotation marks, with their own question mark.

items.sentence: Meena said, "I am hungry."
items.rule: A comma comes before the spoken words; the full stop stays inside the marks.

items.sentence: Meena said that she was hungry.
items.rule: In reported speech "I am" becomes "she was".

items.sentence: Ravi asked me where I was going.
items.rule: A reported question uses statement order and has no question mark.

items.sentence: She said that she [will] come the next day.
items.rule: In reported speech "will" becomes "would".

items.sentence: The teacher told us to open our books.
items.rule: An order is reported with "told" and "to".

items.sentence: I wanted to play, but it was too dark.
items.rule: Two simple sentences joined by "but" make a compound sentence.

items.sentence: She opened the door and the cat ran out.
items.rule: "And" joins two simple sentences into a compound sentence.

items.sentence: You can walk or you can take the bus.
items.rule: "Or" joins two choices.

items.sentence: He studied hard, so he passed the test.
items.rule: "So" joins a cause to its result.

items.sentence: First I brushed my teeth, and then I went to bed.
items.rule: Linking words such as "first" and "then" show the order.

items.sentence: Finally, we reached the top of the hill.
items.rule: "Finally" marks the last event.

items.sentence: After the rain stopped, the children went out to play.
items.rule: "After" shows which event came first.

items.sentence: Later that evening, we watched the fireworks.
items.rule: "Later" moves the story on in time.

items.sentence: What a lovely day it is!
items.rule: An exclamation ends with an exclamation mark.

items.sentence: My birthday is in [july].
items.rule: Months start with a capital letter.

items.sentence: We visited [delhi] last winter.
items.rule: Names of places start with a capital letter.

items.sentence: Yes, I have finished my work.
items.rule: A comma follows "yes" or "no" at the start of an answer.

items.sentence: My uncle, who lives in Pune, is a doctor.
items.rule: Commas go around extra information about a person.

items.sentence: I have [live] here for five years.
items.rule: After "have", use the third form: have lived.

items.sentence: If it rains, we [would] stay at home.
items.rule: A real "if" about the future takes "will".

items.sentence: She has been [wait] for an hour.
items.rule: "Has been" is followed by verb-ing.

items.sentence: [Their] is a parrot on the roof.
items.rule: "There is" points something out; "their" shows belonging.

items.sentence: I am taller [then] my cousin.
items.rule: "Than" compares; "then" is about time.

items.sentence: Please [except] my apology.
items.rule: "Accept" means to take; "except" means leaving out.

items.sentence: The boy who won the race is my cousin.
items.rule: "Who" adds information about a person.

items.sentence: This is the book that I told you about.
items.rule: "That" adds information about a thing.

items.sentence: We read The Jungle [book] in class.
items.rule: The main words in a title start with capital letters.

items.sentence: My favourite film is The Lion [king].
items.rule: The main words in a title start with capital letters.

items.sentence: Our class is reading Malgudi [days] this term.
items.rule: The main words in a title start with capital letters.

items.sentence: The [dogs] tail is wagging; our dog is happy.
items.rule: For one owner, add an apostrophe and s: the dog's tail.

items.sentence: I borrowed my [sisters] pen; I have one sister.
items.rule: For one owner, add an apostrophe and s: my sister's pen.

items.sentence: There are three [dog's] in the park.
items.rule: A plural needs no apostrophe: three dogs.

items.sentence: "Come here," said Mother.
items.rule: The spoken words go inside quotation marks, with a comma before the closing mark.

items.sentence: "I won!" shouted Arun.
items.rule: The exclamation mark belongs to the spoken words, so it stays inside the marks.

items.sentence: Father asked, "Who broke the window?"
items.rule: A comma comes before the spoken words; their question mark stays inside the marks.

items.sentence: My brother and [me] went to the fair.
items.rule: As the subject, use "I": my brother and I went.

items.sentence: The teacher gave the prizes to Ravi and [I].
items.rule: After "to", use "me": to Ravi and me.

items.sentence: We painted the room [ourself].
items.rule: The reflexive form of "we" is "ourselves".

items.sentence: He cut [hisself] while peeling the mango.
items.rule: The reflexive form of "he" is "himself".

items.sentence: She taught [her] to swim; nobody helped.
items.rule: When the doer and the receiver are the same person, use the reflexive: herself.

items.sentence: The students finished [his] work early.
items.rule: A plural noun takes a plural pronoun: the students, their.

items.sentence: The puppy wagged [their] tail.
items.rule: One animal takes "its".

items.sentence: Meena and Ravi forgot [her] books.
items.rule: Two people joined by "and" take "their".

items.sentence: The box of mangoes [are] on the table.
items.rule: The subject is "box", not "mangoes", so the verb is singular.

items.sentence: The boys in the last row [is] talking.
items.rule: The subject is "boys", so the verb is plural.

items.sentence: She opened the door and [walks] in.
items.rule: Keep to one tense: opened, walked.

items.sentence: We went to the beach and [swim] all day.
items.rule: Keep to the past: went, swam.

items.sentence: He picks up the bat and [hit] the ball.
items.rule: Keep to the present: picks, hits.

items.sentence: By the time we arrived, the film had [start].
items.rule: The past perfect is "had" with the third form: had started.

items.sentence: They have [went] home.
items.rule: Go, went, gone: after "have" use gone.

items.sentence: The girl whose bag was lost is crying.
items.rule: "Whose" adds information about what belongs to a person.
